design_detail: Narrative pharmacology review of methamphetamine-induced hyperthermia (Pharmacol Ther 2014;144(1):28–40), by seven authors at West Virginia University, the University of Chicago, Vanderbilt and the CDC's National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health. Sections: normal thermoregulation (anatomy, neurochemistry, body-mass scaling); methamphetamine and temperature regulation, with environmental and disease modulators; clinical considerations, including emergency presentation, diagnosis and symptomatic management; preclinical pharmacological and molecular studies by target system (noradrenaline, dopamine, serotonin, reactive species, immune, miscellaneous) including manipulations that failed; conclusions. No methods section: no search strategy, eligibility criteria or appraisal. 153 references. Two tables: Table 1 contrasts physiological responses to environmental heat with those to high-dose methamphetamine; Table 2 lists compounds tested against hyperthermia in preclinical models with their molecular targets (structures are images). One schematic figure (image). Read as the NIH author manuscript in PMC; the manuscript carries a publisher's disclaimer that it is an unedited accepted version.
can_establish: What was known in 2014 about the mechanisms proposed for methamphetamine-induced hyperthermia, almost entirely from rodent experiments, and which manipulations raised, lowered or did not change body temperature in those models.
cannot_establish: Anything quantitative about hyperthermia in people: no human incidence, no temperature distributions, no case-fatality, no dose–temperature relation and no treatment effect, because the review cites no human series with numbers other than an annual emergency-department count and a clinical threshold, and because the authors themselves state that rodent thermoregulation does not scale to humans.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). The evidence base is overwhelmingly preclinical: rats, mice (including C57BL/6J, ICR and several knockout lines), rhesus macaques, isolated rat hepatocytes and synaptosomes. Human sources cited are a 1970 series of acute high-dose toxic reactions in Haight-Ashbury, a 2002 report of acute liver failure, clinical toxicology and emergency-medicine reviews, a 1978 study of induced hyperthermia in sedated people, and US agency statistics.
sample.selection_effects: Selection of sources is unstated and cannot be audited. The review is weighted towards the authors' own programme: several cited studies of sigma-receptor compounds against methamphetamine hyperthermia are by the corresponding author's group (AC927, AZ66, CM156, SN79), and two authors (Miller, O'Callaghan) wrote several of the cited temperature-and-neurotoxicity studies in mice.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable at review level; the cited animal studies administered known amounts under controlled conditions, which the review does not tabulate.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Reported only as study conditions and rarely: the review states that lower, stimulant amounts do not have significant effects on body temperature while high amounts can produce lethal hyperthermia, and gives exactly one animal dose (a bolus of 30 mg/kg in ICR mice in a study where two dopamine antagonists failed to block the temperature rise). Doses, schedules and ambient temperatures of the other cited experiments are not given, although ambient temperature is repeatedly named as decisive (protective effects of several drugs disappeared at 28.5, 29 or 33 degrees C; one inhibitor worked only at 20 degrees C).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed as a confounder. Co-exposure is discussed only mechanistically (the comparison with MDMA, and amphetamine formed as a metabolite being itself capable of raising temperature).

comparison.controls: Not applicable at review level. The cited experiments compare treated with untreated animals, knockout with wild-type mice, or drug-pretreated with vehicle-pretreated animals.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable (experimental literature). For the human statements, no comparison group is described anywhere.

outcomes.instruments: Not specified at review level: core or brain temperature in animals, measured by means the review does not describe; in the clinical sections, core body temperature and the laboratory and histological markers of liver injury (AST, ALT, histopathology).
outcomes.validity_norms: The review notes a clinical threshold: hyperthermia is diagnosed when core temperature exceeds 40 degrees C, at which point thermoregulation is said to fail.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Hyperthermia' is used for any drug-induced elevation of body or brain temperature in animals and for the clinical syndrome in people, without a stated quantitative criterion for the animal studies. The review explicitly distinguishes hyperthermia from fever and notes that anti-inflammatory drugs do not affect it.

analysis.effect_sizes: None computed, and almost none reported: no temperature changes in degrees, no sample sizes, no intervals and no test statistics are given for any cited experiment, with one exception (tryptophan hydroxylase 2 knockout mice lacking brain serotonin showed a hyperthermic response about 1 degree C greater than controls). Effects are described only as attenuation, prevention, no significant effect or enhancement. Two human figures: an estimated 94,000 US emergency-department admissions a year attributed to methamphetamine (a 2011 agency source) and 65% of heat-related deaths resulting from exposure to excessive heat (a 2006 CDC report, which is a statement about heat deaths generally, not about methamphetamine).
analysis.selective_reporting: Cannot be assessed for source selection, but the review is unusually explicit about negative results: a whole section lists manipulations that did not change methamphetamine-induced hyperthermia (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, an interleukin-1 receptor antagonist, several neuroprotective agents, interleukin-6 knockout), and divergent findings are reported (dopamine antagonists failing in one mouse study; a serotonin-enhancing drug lowering rather than raising temperature; a radical scavenger that blocks peroxynitrite but not hyperthermia).

interpretation_gap.results_show: A mechanistic literature in rodents in which many unrelated interventions lower methamphetamine-induced hyperthermia and several expected ones do not; no single mechanism is identified; ambient temperature, group housing, stress and exercise modulate the effect; and the relationship between temperature, neurotoxicity and death is correlational in animals. The human content is a clinical description of presentation and symptomatic cooling, with no numbers beyond an annual admission count and the 40 degrees C threshold.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that reports of methamphetamine-related emergency room visits suggest elevated body temperature is a universal presenting symptom, and the introduction repeats 'universal'. No study, proportion or temperature distribution supports this in the text; the citation given for the admission count is an agency fact sheet on drug-related emergency visits. The abstract also says lethal overdoses are generally associated with extreme hyperthermia, again without a source reporting temperatures at death. By contrast, the body is careful: it says the mechanisms are largely unknown and relatively unexplored, that the mechanistic relationship between methamphetamine, hyperthermia, neurotoxicity and mortality has not been established, that rodent-to-human extrapolation is limited by body-mass scaling, and that it is unknown whether cooling improves outcomes in methamphetamine overdose because no prospective studies exist. The gap is therefore confined to the two universality claims in the abstract, which are the sentences most likely to be quoted.

timeline.event: Greenblatt & Osterberg: lethality of stimulants greater in grouped than isolated mice ('aggregate toxicity'), cited here as the origin of the social-housing effect
Smith & Fischer: 310 cases of acute high-dose methamphetamine toxicity in Haight-Ashbury, cited here for hepatitis as the second commonest presenting complaint

Bowyer et al. and Miller & O'Callaghan: lowering ambient temperature prevents methamphetamine hyperthermia and attenuates dopaminergic neurotoxicity in rodents, the finding on which the temperature-neurotoxicity link rests
Albers & Sonsalla: pharmacological profile of agents protective and non-protective against methamphetamine hyperthermia in mice, the single most-cited source in this review's drug sections
Numachi et al.: dopamine transporter knockout mice show only a modest, non-significant reduction in hyperthermia but a higher lethal dose; serotonin transporter knockout mice show no change
Ito et al.: dopamine D1 and D2 knockout mice show reduced hyperthermia and reduced lethality; surviving animals had lower temperatures than those that died
Thomas et al.: reducing brain serotonin pharmacologically attenuates hyperthermia, while mice genetically lacking brain serotonin show hyperthermia about 1 degree C greater

replication.where_it_stands: Still the standard mechanistic reference on methamphetamine hyperthermia, and useful chiefly for its negative results and its explicit statement that no mechanism, and no specific treatment, has been established. It supports no numerical claim about people; the clinical toxicology reviews it cites (Albertson 1999; Schep 2010) and primary emergency-department series would be needed for that.

funding.funder: National Institutes of Health grants DA013978 and GM081741 supported some of the described studies and the authors (Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors state they have no conflicts of interest to disclose (Footnotes, Declaration of interest).
funding.affiliations_note: West Virginia University School of Pharmacy and Center for Neuroscience, Department of Neurosurgery; University of Chicago; Vanderbilt University; and the CDC's National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health. The sigma-receptor compounds presented in Table 2 as potential therapeutic options come from the corresponding author's own research programme, funded by the NIH grants acknowledged here; recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: For the human question: a prospective emergency-department cohort of people presenting after methamphetamine use that records core temperature on arrival for every patient, with outcomes, so that the frequency and distribution of hyperthermia and its relation to death can be estimated rather than asserted. For the mechanism: experiments that separate temperature from neurotoxicity, in species whose thermoregulation resembles human thermoregulation, using local rather than systemic manipulation to locate the peripheral and central sites involved, with ambient temperature reported as a controlled variable.

domains.note: No methods section, search, dates or criteria; the paper moves straight from the introduction to thermoregulatory physiology, and how its references were chosen is never stated.

No methodological appraisal of any cited study: sample sizes, randomization, blinding, doses and effect magnitudes are almost never reported, so the animal literature that carries the review is never weighed the way SYRCLE would weigh it. Against that, the review is explicit about the limits of the evidence as a body: a whole subsection on body-mass scaling and why rodent thermoregulation does not extrapolate to humans, repeated notes that effects differ between rats and mice and with ambient temperature, the statement that no manipulation has produced a clear picture of how monoamines are involved, and the observation that the plasma-serotonin and body-temperature association was never examined.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Much of the evidence is other groups' work, but the reference list carries repeated citations of the authors' own studies (the corresponding author and two co-authors appear many times), two co-authors are the source of several of the temperature-and-neurotoxicity results relied on, and the four sigma-receptor compounds that Table 2 offers among potential pharmacotherapy options come from the corresponding author's own programme.

The body is careful, marking what is unknown or unexplored and labelling proposed mechanisms as proposed. The abstract is not: it states that elevated body temperature is a universal presenting symptom in methamphetamine-related emergency visits and that lethal overdoses are generally associated with extreme hyperthermia, neither of which the body supports with a human series, and the statement about emergency presentations rests on an in-text citation that has no entry in the reference list. Section 3.2 also extends the argument to children and adults treated for amphetamine salts for ADHD and to sport in hot weather, with no evidence offered.

domains.domain: Balance of positive against null and contradictory mechanistic findings
domains.note: Negative and contradictory results are given their own space: a dedicated subsection on manipulations that do not affect methamphetamine hyperthermia (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, an interleukin-1 receptor antagonist, several neuroprotective agents), species reversals reported wherever they occur, and the unexplained protective effect of fenfluramine left unexplained.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3), so the editors' narrative-review checklist is used. The absence of any search or selection method fixes that domain at high and therefore the overall judgment at high, since the overall can be no milder than the worst domain. Within that limit this is a careful mechanistic survey: it is balanced about null findings, open about species differences and body-mass scaling, and sceptical about its own evidence base. Its weaknesses for this encyclopedia are that it reports almost no magnitudes, so nothing in it can anchor a quantitative claim; that its two human generalizations sit in the abstract unsupported by the body; and that some of its own citations do not support the statements they are attached to. Cite it for the map of mechanisms tested and for its negative findings, and take every number from the primary study.

key_findings.finding: The review states that methamphetamine at lower, stimulant amounts does not have significant effects on body temperature, while high amounts can produce lethal hyperthermia; the mechanisms combine increased heat production (central and skeletal-muscle activation) with impaired heat loss (vasoconstriction).
key_findings.locator: 3. METH and temperature regulation, 1st paragraph; 3.1 Body temperature dysregulation by METH; Figure 1 legend; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Table 1 contrasts the response to environmental heat (hypothalamic heat-sensitive neuron activation; reduced metabolic and muscle activity; increased skin blood flow and sweating) with the response to high-dose methamphetamine (raised brain temperature, heat-shock protein expression, vasoconstriction and piloerection, with saliva spreading as the only heat-loss mechanism listed in animals).
key_findings.note: The table is a conceptual summary without data, and the animal items (piloerection, saliva spreading) do not transfer to people.

key_findings.finding: Rodent-to-human extrapolation is limited: small animals have a large surface-area-to-volume ratio and regulate surface temperature by passive heat dissipation and metabolic change, whereas humans depend on sweating and peripheral vasomotor mechanisms, making rodents more vulnerable to ambient temperature than humans.

Modulators of the temperature response in animals: raising ambient temperature enhances and cold prevents methamphetamine hyperthermia and attenuates oxidation products and neurotoxicity; group housing increases toxicity and lethality ('aggregate toxicity'), with brain temperature rising before and above body temperature; unpredictable stress enhances hyperthermia in rats (preventable by a 5-HT2 antagonist) while restraint stress in mice lowers body temperature and confers resistance to dopaminergic neurotoxicity.
key_findings.locator: 3.2 Modulators of thermoregulation and METH hyperthermia

key_findings.finding: Clinical description: the commonest presenting feature in emergency departments after a methamphetamine overdose is said to be extreme hyperthermia, which can be lethal untreated; other features listed are hypertension, tachycardia, breathlessness, chest pain, agitation, altered mental status, pupil dilation, shivering and possible seizures. Hyperthermia is diagnosed clinically above a core temperature of 40 degrees C.
key_findings.note: No proportions, temperature distributions or case numbers are given; the symptom list is cited to a 1999 clinical review.

key_findings.finding: No approved pharmacotherapy exists for methamphetamine hyperthermia; management is symptomatic cooling, and the authors state it is unknown whether cooling improves outcomes in methamphetamine overdose because no prospective studies have been done.
key_findings.locator: 4.2 Treatment of METH hyperthermia, 2nd paragraph; 6. Summary and conclusions, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Liver: hepatitis was the second commonest presenting complaint in a 1970 series of acute toxic reactions; acute liver damage has been reported without viral hepatitis; in a rat binge model, aminotransferases rose with histopathological changes; raising temperature exogenously worsened methamphetamine hepatotoxicity in vitro, and hyperthermia contributed to liver damage and raised peripheral ammonia in vivo.
key_findings.locator: 4.3 Clinical consequences of METH hyperthermia, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: No numbers from the human reports are given; the mechanistic evidence is from rats and isolated hepatocytes.

key_findings.finding: Damage to dopaminergic nerve terminals in rats and mice tracks core temperature: raising ambient temperature worsens it, lowering core temperature by pharmacological, genetic or physiological means reduces it, and raising brain methamphetamine levels has no neurotoxic effect if body temperature is kept low. The authors state that elevated temperature appears to be an obligatory component of neurotoxicity in these models but that the controlling mechanism is unknown and the relationship between methamphetamine, hyperthermia, neurotoxicity and mortality has not been established.
key_findings.locator: 4.3 Clinical consequences of METH hyperthermia, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Catecholamines: peripheral chemical sympathectomy with 6-hydroxydopamine blocked methamphetamine hyperthermia, and blocking catecholamine synthesis with alpha-methyl-p-tyrosine attenuated it in rats but not mice, and in rats only at room temperature, not at a raised ambient temperature of 28.5 degrees C. Within the noradrenaline section the species differ: the beta-adrenoceptor antagonist propranolol prevented methamphetamine hyperthermia in mice, whereas the series supporting noradrenaline-driven thermogenesis in skeletal muscle under glucocorticoid permission is in rats, where sympathectomy or adrenalectomy prevented hyperthermia, dexamethasone restored it in adrenalectomized animals, and the muscle calcium-release inhibitor dantrolene prevented it. The receptor subtypes responsible are unidentified.
key_findings.locator: 5.1 Monoaminergic systems, 2nd–3rd paragraphs; 5.1.1 Norepinephrine systems, 2nd paragraph (propranolol, mice) and 3rd paragraph (sympathectomy, adrenalectomy, glucocorticoid and dantrolene series, rats)

key_findings.finding: Dopamine: methamphetamine failed to produce hyperthermia in dopamine D2 knockout mice; D2 and D1 antagonists attenuated it, but the protection was lost at higher ambient temperatures (29 and 33 degrees C), and in one study in ICR mice a D1 and a D2 antagonist did not attenuate the temperature rise after a 30 mg/kg bolus. In D1 and D2 knockout mice both hyperthermia and lethality were reduced, and in both knockout and wild-type groups animals that survived had lower temperatures than those that died. Dopamine transporter knockout mice showed only a modest, non-significant reduction in hyperthermia but a higher lethal dose.
key_findings.note: This is the review's only direct temperature-mortality observation, and it is in mice.

key_findings.finding: Serotonin: depleting brain serotonin pharmacologically attenuated hyperthermia in mice, yet mice genetically lacking brain serotonin showed a hyperthermic response about 1 degree C greater, which the authors read as compensation by other systems; serotonin transporter knockout mice showed unchanged hyperthermia. A 5-HT1A antagonist blocked the temperature rise while a 5-HT1A agonist did not attenuate it, and a serotonin-releasing drug paradoxically reduced hyperthermia. The authors conclude serotonin modulates but is not required.

Reactive species: an antioxidant, melatonin and an iron chelator each attenuated hyperthermia in rodents, and mice lacking neuronal nitric oxide synthase resisted it, but nitric oxide synthase inhibitors worked only at 20 degrees C and not at normal or raised ambient temperature, and one radical scavenger blocked peroxynitrite without affecting temperature. Older rats were more sensitive than young rats to peroxynitrite formation and to the hyperthermic and lethal effects.

Other targets: a protein kinase C delta inhibitor reduced hyperthermia and knockout mice resisted it; sigma-receptor antagonists (AC927, AZ66, CM156, SN79) attenuated hyperthermia in mice; an anticonvulsant attenuated it without changing temperature alone; a GABA transaminase inhibitor, an NMDA antagonist and ibogaine reduced it but caused hypothermia alone; systemic but not intracerebroventricular interferon-gamma reduced it, as did an immunosuppressive antibiotic that inhibits a transcription-factor family.
key_findings.note: Table 2 lists these compounds with their molecular targets; chemical structures are images and were not extracted.

key_findings.finding: Manipulations without effect on methamphetamine hyperthermia: ibuprofen and aspirin in mice; an interleukin-1 receptor antagonist (which nevertheless reduced deaths); and a list of neuroprotective agents and genetic modifications including edaravone, carnosine, minocycline, memantine, an alpha-7 nicotinic antagonist, calcitriol, ketamine and interleukin-6 knockout. Hypothalamic interleukin-1 beta expression did not correlate with body temperature.
key_findings.locator: 5.5 Mechanisms that do not affect METH hyperthermia
key_findings.note: These negative results separate hyperthermia from fever and separate neuroprotection from temperature control.

key_findings.finding: Conclusion as drawn by the authors: no single mechanism underlies methamphetamine hyperthermia, no pharmacological profile predicts protection, broad classes of drugs with no clear thermoregulatory action can act as countermeasures in animals, and most studies used systemic administration or whole-body knockouts so central and peripheral sites cannot be separated; peripheral mechanisms and muscle heat generation appear important.

The review states that it is unclear whether the maximum methamphetamine-induced rise in body temperature is related specifically to peak plasma concentration or rather to cumulative exposure, so no dose-temperature relation is established. It also notes that metabolites may contribute to a sustained hyperthermic effect, amphetamine having been reported to raise body temperature on its own.
key_findings.locator: 4.1 Pharmacokinetic parameters of METH, 1st paragraph (last sentence) and 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Recorded as the authors' own acknowledgement that no dose-temperature relation exists in this literature; it supports the card's cannot_establish. Route and bioavailability figures from the same paragraph are deliberately not extracted, as no claim needs them.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's statement that elevated body temperature is a universal presenting symptom of methamphetamine-related emergency room visits has no supporting data anywhere in the text; the only citation near the equivalent sentence in the introduction is an agency fact sheet on drug-related emergency visits used for the figure of about 94,000 admissions a year.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not citable. Any claim about how often people presenting after methamphetamine use are hyperthermic needs an emergency-department series that measured temperature in all patients.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's statement that lethal overdoses are generally associated with extreme hyperthermia is likewise unsupported in the text; the only temperature-mortality data given are from mice (survivors had lower temperatures than animals that died).
reporting_issues.consequence: The human generalization rests on animal data; claims must say so.

reporting_issues.issue: In section 3.2, 1st paragraph, the statement that 65% of heat-related deaths result from exposure to excessive heat is cited to a CDC report on heat-related deaths in general and concerns neither methamphetamine nor drug-related deaths; the review then infers, by analogy with MDMA, that the clinical condition would be expected to be greatly exaggerated with methamphetamine co-exposure.
reporting_issues.consequence: An expectation by analogy, not a finding; the figure does not belong in any methamphetamine claim.

reporting_issues.issue: Two in-text citations have no matching entry in the reference list: 'Bowyer et al., 1984' and 'Bowyer et al., 1995' (the list contains Bowyer et al. 1992, 1994 and 2013 and Bowyer & Holson 1995). The 1984 citation supports the statement that hyperthermia is the major presenting symptom in emergency rooms, and the 1995 citation supports several statements about the temperature dependence of neurotoxicity.
reporting_issues.consequence: The emergency-room statement cannot be traced to a source at all; the neurotoxicity statements probably intend Bowyer & Holson (1995), a book chapter.

reporting_issues.issue: Effect magnitudes are absent throughout: no cited experiment is reported with a sample size, a temperature change in degrees, an interval or a test statistic, except one roughly 1 degree C enhancement in serotonin-deficient mice. Animal doses and ambient temperatures are given only sporadically, while the review itself shows that ambient temperature determines whether a drug protects.
reporting_issues.consequence: Nothing in this review can anchor a quantitative claim; each primary study must be read for its conditions and magnitudes.

reporting_issues.issue: Statements about serotonin manipulation are internally confusing: pharmacological inhibition of tryptophan hydroxylase is said to attenuate hyperthermia, while 'treatment of mice with tryptophan hydroxylase' (apparently a word missing, probably an inhibitor of a specific isoform) is said not to alter it, in the same sentence as the knockout result.
reporting_issues.consequence: The serotonin section cannot be paraphrased precisely from this text; the primary study must be read.

reporting_issues.issue: Two antipsychotic drug names are given in non-standard spellings in the text and in Table 2 ('risperidol'; 'p-cholorphenyl-alanine' in Table 2 versus 'p-chlorophenylalanine' in the text), and one author's surname is spelled two ways in the reference list and text.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical only, but the compound identities should be confirmed from the primary studies before any claim names a drug.

reporting_issues.issue: Read from the NIH author manuscript, which carries a publisher's disclaimer that it is an unedited accepted version; printed pagination is not shown in the HTML. The PMC line gives the final edited form as Pharmacol Ther 2014 May 14;144(1):28-40, so the only date visible in this save is 14 May 2014; the first reader also recorded an October 2014 print issue, which this reading could not check.
reporting_issues.consequence: Anchors are to sections of the author manuscript rather than printed pages; the citation year is 2014 on either date.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 files vasoconstriction and piloerection in animals under activation of heat production mechanisms in the methamphetamine column, while section 2 lists vasoconstriction and insulation (including piloerection in furred animals) among heat retention strategies, and section 3.1 describes methamphetamine-induced vasoconstriction as contributing to hyperthermia by preventing heat dissipation. Table 1 also files saliva spreading in animals under activation of heat loss mechanisms for methamphetamine, which matches the text.
reporting_issues.consequence: The table contradicts the paper's own physiology: vasoconstriction retains heat and blocks dissipation rather than producing it. Table 1 is the part of this review most likely to be reused, so its headings should not be carried over as the paper's classification of mechanisms.

reporting_issues.issue: Several citations in section 3.1 do not support the statements they are attached to. The sentence that methamphetamine causes vasoconstriction carries four references: a study of the autonomic thermoregulatory response of the rat to MDMA, an emergency-department study of the frequency of acute coronary syndrome in people presenting with chest pain after methamphetamine use, a case report of methamphetamine-induced myocardial infarction with raised troponin, and a study of electrocardiographic abnormalities. None measured vasoconstriction, and the first concerns a different drug. The statement about drooling and saliva spreading in methamphetamine-treated animals cites a general review of central thermoregulatory pathways.
reporting_issues.consequence: Vasoconstriction is central to the review's account of how methamphetamine raises body temperature, and the citations given do not evidence it. Any claim about methamphetamine-induced vasoconstriction needs a study that measured it; this belongs with the citation problems already recorded for this source.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 gives the molecular target of fenfluramine as a serotonin-transporter inhibitor, while the text (5.1.3, 7th paragraph) describes it as enhancing serotonin function through several mechanisms, calls it a serotonin indirect agonist, and notes that it also enhances noradrenaline release, which the authors suggest may explain its protective effect against methamphetamine hyperthermia.
reporting_issues.consequence: A text-table inconsistency of the same kind as the other table problems on this card. The pharmacology in Table 2 should not be quoted without reading the matching passage, and fenfluramine's mechanism in this context is explicitly unresolved in the text.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 3.2, 3rd paragraph, extends the heat argument from methamphetamine to children and adults treated with a mixture of amphetamine salts for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, who are said to be prone to more difficulty in extreme temperature situations such as playing sport in hot summer months. No evidence is cited for that sentence, and no study of people taking prescribed stimulants is reported anywhere in the review.
reporting_issues.consequence: An unevidenced clinical extrapolation to a different substance and a different population, including children. It should not be carried into any monograph from this review.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC4700537 (NIH author manuscript; all sections, Tables 1 and 2 rendered as text, the Figure 1 legend, abbreviations list, acknowledgments, declaration of interest, publisher's disclaimer, author affiliations and the full 153-entry reference list; Figure 1 and the chemical structures in Table 2 are images and were not extracted; no supplementary material)

disagreements.first_pass: Catecholamines: peripheral chemical sympathectomy or adrenalectomy prevented methamphetamine hyperthermia in rats, and blocking catecholamine synthesis attenuated it in rats but not mice and only at room temperature, not at 28.5 degrees C. A beta-adrenoceptor antagonist and a muscle calcium-release inhibitor each prevented hyperthermia, supporting noradrenaline-driven thermogenesis in skeletal muscle under glucocorticoid permission; the receptor subtypes are unidentified.
disagreements.reviewer: species are conflated in the second half: the beta-adrenoceptor result (propranolol, Albers & Sonsalla 1995, 5.1.1 ¶2) is in mice, while the sympathectomy, adrenalectomy, glucocorticoid and muscle calcium-release results (Makisumi 1998, 5.1.1 ¶3) are in rats, and it is that rat series alone that supports the muscle-thermogenesis reading
disagreements.resolution: Accepted and rewritten with the species attached to each result. Checked at 5.1.1: ¶2 reports propranolol preventing methamphetamine hyperthermia in laboratory mice; ¶3 reports the 6-hydroxydopamine sympathectomy, adrenalectomy, dexamethasone and dantrolene results, all from one rat series, and it is that series the review reads as methamphetamine stimulating noradrenaline release and so thermogenesis in skeletal muscle under the permissive control of glucocorticoids. The first half is confirmed at 5.1 ¶2-3. The locator now names the paragraphs separately.

disagreements.reviewer: content confirmed, locator off by one at the start: the serotonin-depletion result and the roughly 1 degree C greater response in mice lacking brain serotonin are in 5.1.3 ¶3, not ¶4 (¶4 is the plasma-serotonin paragraph, which the finding does not cover); the right span is ¶3 and ¶5 to ¶8
disagreements.resolution: Corrected to 3rd paragraph and 5th to 8th paragraphs. Checked in the source: 5.1.3 ¶3 carries both the p-chlorophenylalanine depletion result in mice and the enhanced hyperthermic response of about 1 degree C in tryptophan hydroxylase 2 knockout mice; ¶4 is about dose-dependent rises in plasma serotonin in rats, whose relation to body temperature the review says was not examined; ¶5 is the serotonin-transporter knockout result, ¶6 the 5-HT1A antagonist and agonist results, ¶7 fenfluramine and ¶8 the conclusion that serotonin modulates but is not required.

disagreements.first_pass: Read from the NIH author manuscript, which carries a publisher's disclaimer that it is an unedited accepted version; printed pagination (Pharmacol Ther 2014;144(1):28–40) is not shown in the HTML, and the PMC header gives the online date 14 May 2014 while the issue date is October 2014.
disagreements.reviewer: partly-confirmed: the author manuscript, the disclaimer, the absence of printed pagination and the 14 May 2014 header date are confirmed; that the print issue is October 2014 could not be checked from the saved text

The citation year is 2014 either way, as the issue already said.

disagreements.first_pass: AMSTAR 2 (14 items recorded, overall critically-low confidence)
disagreements.reviewer: wrong instrument: a narrative review takes the editors' narrative-review checklist (none-applicable); proposed judgments high / high / some-concerns / some-concerns / low, overall high
disagreements.resolution: Re-appraised with the editors' narrative-review checklist (METHODS §5.3, modelled on sc_kish_2017). I agree with the second reader on four domains and differ on one: appraisal of the cited studies, which I judge some concerns rather than high, because the review names the limits of its evidence base at length (a subsection on body-mass scaling, species reversals, manipulations that produced no clear picture, an association never tested) even though it never appraises an individual study, which is the standard the model card sc_kish_2017 records as some concerns. The disagreement is listed for the senior author. Overall high, the worst domain, which is the absent search.

disagreements.resolution: Added as a reporting issue. All three places checked: Table 1 heading 3 in the methamphetamine column; section 2, 2nd heat paragraph, listing vasoconstriction and insulation as heat retention strategies; section 3.1, 1st paragraph, where vasoconstriction contributes to hyperthermia by preventing heat dissipation in the periphery.
